strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of amortised Bayesian inference: adapting to changing priors while retaining a posterior representation that can be reused as the next prior in sequential inference. This is a meaningful problem, and the GMM-token transformer construction is a plausible and useful architectural idea.

The method is technically coherent: representing priors/posteriors as unordered GMM component tokens matches the permutation symmetry of mixtures, cross-attention to observations is natural, and the sample-based NLL objective is appropriately connected to expected posterior KL up to constants.

The empirical section is broader than many papers in this area, covering an analytically tractable conjugate case, GP predictive/hyperposterior inference, quantum parameter inference, and two sequential filtering settings. The sequential experiments are especially relevant to the claimed advantage over fixed-prior amortised methods.

The paper includes useful ablations on prior loss, meta-prior shift, GMM component count, dimensional scaling, and sequential error accumulation. The limitations section is reasonably honest about training cost, meta-prior specification, GMM scaling, and recursive error accumulation.
Presentation is generally clear, with helpful diagrams and tables. The appendix provides many implementation and training details, including model sizes, training times, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The evaluation is still mostly on author-designed synthetic or semi-synthetic problems. The paper makes broad claims about real-world sensor fusion and practical Bayesian inference, but there is no evaluation on established public benchmarks or real datasets where modelling assumptions and meta-priors are not controlled by the authors.

Baseline comparisons are not always fully convincing. PFNs are disadvantaged by lack of explicit prior conditioning, TabPFNv2 is used in a somewhat nonstandard way by encoding prior parameters as observations, and ACE appears to be adapted with GMM heads and fixed latent choices. The paper would benefit from stronger prior-flexible SBI baselines such as neural posterior/ratio estimators trained over priors, flow-based approaches, or BayesFlow-style methods under comparable amortisation budgets.

Several claims are overstated. The architecture is said to learn arbitrary distribution-to-distribution mappings, but the practical method is constrained by a fixed-size full-covariance GMM, chosen warping maps, and a learned meta-prior distribution. Generalisation outside the meta-prior is only lightly probed and remains a major limitation.

The sequential inference results are promising but not definitive. Particle filters are treated as near-ground truth in places, yet in the high-dimensional stochastic volatility experiment the PF density approximation is changed to a moment-matched Gaussian for memory reasons, complicating the accuracy comparison. There is also no comparison to more advanced SMC variants, assumed-density filters, ensemble Kalman methods, or learned filtering baselines.

There appears to be a sign inconsistency or typo in Algorithm 1: the displayed empirical loss contains '- log q_theta(f(x_i)|phi_i) + log q_theta(f(x_i)|z_i,phi_i)', whereas the surrounding text defines a sum of negative log prior and negative log posterior terms. If not a typo, this would be a serious objective error; if a typo, it should be fixed for reproducibility.

Reproducibility is partial. The manuscript says code is available on GitHub, but the provided text does not include a visible URL or release details. Important choices such as warping functions, exact baseline tuning, random seeds, evaluation sample sizes for all experiments, and confidence interval computation are not always specified in enough detail to independently reproduce the reported numbers.

The ethical/impact discussion is very minimal. This is not a major concern for the method itself, but sequential inference and sensor-fusion applications can have safety-critical uses; a brief discussion of calibration failure, out-of-distribution priors, and deployment risk would be appropriate.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: amortized Bayesian inference with test-time prior variation and recursive/sequential use, which is a genuine limitation of many PFN/SBI-style methods.
Representing priors and posteriors as unordered GMM component tokens is a plausible architectural idea, and the permutation-equivariant transformer design is natural for this representation.

The manuscript includes several experiments beyond a toy conjugate case, including GP hyperposterior inference, a quantum-parameter example, and sequential filtering tasks; the reported speedups over iterative methods are potentially useful if reproducible.

The paper does include some limitations and ablations, including meta-prior misspecification, dimensional scaling, prior-loss ablation, GMM component-count generalization, and error accumulation over sequence depth.
weaknesses: The central claims are substantially overextended. The paper repeatedly claims arbitrary distribution-to-distribution mappings and broad Bayesian inference capability, but the method is trained per problem family under a specified meta-prior and evaluated only on synthetic or highly controlled generative settings. This does not establish general prior adaptation or arbitrary distribution mapping.

The empirical evidence is not convincing enough for the strength of the claims. Most tasks are designed by the authors with known simulators and train/test distributions; there is little evidence on established benchmark suites, real datasets, or difficult out-of-distribution prior changes. The sequential examples are interesting but remain synthetic and use assumed model dynamics/likelihoods.

Baseline comparisons appear potentially unfair or underdeveloped. PFNs are intentionally deprived of explicit prior information except through marginalization in some comparisons; TabPFNv2 is used in settings outside its intended design; SVI/MCMC settings appear weak or unstable; ACE is modified but not deeply tuned. The paper often interprets baseline failure as evidence for DT rather than demonstrating that strong prior-flexible baselines were fairly adapted.

The theoretical contribution is thin. Proposition 3.1 is essentially the standard expected negative log-likelihood/KL identity under a change of variables. Universality of GMMs and transformers does not imply learnability, calibration, sequential stability, or reliable approximation with small component counts in the settings claimed.

There is a serious presentation/soundness ambiguity in Algorithm 1: the displayed empirical loss appears to use a positive posterior log-density term rather than a negative log-density term, contradicting the surrounding text and objective. If this is not merely a typo, the training objective is wrong; if it is a typo, it is still a concerning reproducibility issue in the core algorithm.

The treatment of sequential inference is incomplete. The claimed approximate conjugacy is mostly architectural rather than theoretically characterized, and error accumulation is only lightly probed. There is no rigorous analysis of when recursively feeding approximate GMM posteriors remains stable or calibrated.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance as written. The paper says code is available on GitHub but provides no visible URL in the manuscript text I inspected, and many implementation details are described only qualitatively or as limited manual tuning. Critical choices such as meta-priors, transformations, baseline tuning, particle counts, and model selection need clearer, auditable specification.

The ethics/impact statement is perfunctory: it states there are no consequences worth highlighting, despite applications to sensor fusion, tracking, finance-like stochastic volatility, and quantum systems. Potential misuse, deployment risks under model misspecification, and overconfident approximate inference are not meaningfully discussed.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful idea: represent priors and posteriors as GMM token sequences and learn a transformer mapping that conditions on observations while preserving the same distribution family. This directly addresses prior-flexible amortized inference and makes sequential reuse of posteriors as priors natural.

The core training objective is well motivated: the sample-based NLL objective is connected to expected posterior KL up to constants, and the additional prior reconstruction loss is justified and ablated. The prior-loss ablation is convincing for the claimed approximate latent-space conjugacy.

The empirical evaluation is broad for a methods paper, covering an analytically tractable conjugate case, GP predictive/hyperposterior inference, quantum parameter inference, and two sequential filtering settings. The results consistently show strong NLL/KL performance and large test-time speed advantages over iterative baselines.

The comparison to prior-flexible and amortized baselines such as PFN/TabPFN/ACE, plus classical SVI/MCMC/EKF/PF where appropriate, makes the contribution easier to position. The paper also reports confidence intervals, runtimes, model sizes, training costs, and several useful ablations.

The limitations section is unusually concrete: it discusses meta-prior coverage, high-dimensional GMM costs, manual tuning, and sequential error accumulation, with supplementary experiments probing some of these concerns.
weaknesses: Several claims are broader than the evidence supports. The architecture is described as learning arbitrary distribution-to-distribution mappings, but the demonstrated regime is modest-dimensional and constrained to GMM outputs with hand-chosen warps/meta-priors. High-dimensional behavior beyond 10-24 latent dimensions remains largely unvalidated.

The experimental tasks are all synthetic or simulator-defined. They are well designed, but the paper would be stronger with at least one real-data Bayesian workflow or a more standard benchmark from SBI/filtering to test whether the meta-prior assumptions and amortization benefits transfer outside controlled generators.

Baseline fairness is somewhat uncertain. PFNs are said to marginalize over the meta-prior and are expected to fail under wide meta-priors; this is informative, but it may understate what a prior-conditioned PFN-style model or stronger flow/SBI baseline could do. Some competitors appear adapted in nonstandard ways, and the paper does not fully explore stronger prior-aware variants.

The sequential experiments are promising but not definitive. Particle filters are treated as near-ground truth in places, yet the appendix notes substitutions such as moment-matched Gaussians for large particle counts because of memory constraints. Offline DT training cost is reported separately but not integrated into the sequential comparison.

Reproducibility is decent but incomplete from the manuscript alone. Hyperparameters and training times are reported, but details such as seeds, exact tuning protocol, code release link/commit, and full baseline configurations are limited. The statement that code is available on GitHub is not enough for archival reproducibility.

There are presentation issues that could confuse implementation: Algorithm 1 appears to have a sign ambiguity or typo in the combined loss, writing the posterior term with a plus log-density where the text defines a negative log-likelihood. There are also minor typos and some overconfident wording in the conclusions.

The ethics/impact statement is minimal. The method targets sensor fusion and potentially scientific/decision systems where miscalibrated uncertainty can matter; a short discussion of risks from meta-prior misspecification, overconfident deployment, and monitoring would be appropriate.
